To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the ecosystem functioning dimension in biodiversity conservation can be addressed by using remote sensing.

1) remote sensing provides accurate and spatially explicit measurements of ecosystem functioning that may be used to aid conservation science and management; 2) remote sensing techniques can be adapted to address conservation questions; and 3) the use of remotely sensed information in conservation practice is a feasible and promising avenue for the future of conservation science and management.
remote sensing provides a unique tool for the assessment of ecosystem functioning and that it is an essential component of conservation science and practice.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how to use remote sensing to quantify ecosystem functioning in order to aid conservation science and management.
the use of satellite remote sensing as a tool for the conservation of biodiversity and ecosystem processes.
how remote sensing may contribute to the conservation science of the 21st century.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ecosystem functioning approach is a powerful and promising tool for conservation science and practice, which is still underutilized.
the ecosystem functioning dimension is a critical component in the conservation of biodiversity and ecosystems.
conservation biology and remote sensing science can benefit greatly from each other.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ecosystem functioning dimension in remote sensing is a powerful tool that can be used to improve the conservation of biodiversity.
remote sensing has the potential to provide a new set of tools and information to support conservation science and practice.
the use of remotely sensed data is a promising tool that can help conservation biologists in the assessment of ecosystem processes.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the integration of remote sensing into conservation science and practice is not a distant possibility but a present reality that is already yielding important results and that is expected to grow rapidly.
the use of remote sensing to quantify ecosystem functions is a powerful approach that should be integrated into the conservation planning and management toolbox.

conservation science and practice will benefit from the integration of remote sensing techniques that quantify ecosystem functioning into the traditional use of remote sensing in biodiversity conservation.
